articles.title: Finland's Stubb credits Trump for pushing Ukraine peace talks while dismissing Russian invasion fears
articles.summary: Finnish President Alexander Stubb credits Trump with pushing for Russia-Ukraine war peace and says Finland is fully prepared for any Moscow threat.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS — As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Russia could take its war beyond Ukraine, Finnish President Alexander Stubb is striking a markedly calmer tone — saying Finland is prepared for Moscow and crediting President Donald Trump with pushing harder for a negotiated end to the war. "I think we're certainly in a better place than we were before President Trump started," Stubb told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "He's doubled down in the past year and a half to try to find a solution for peace with negotiators such as Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and many others." Stubb, who has been closely involved in the diplomatic effort, said he and Norway’s prime minister have worked largely "in the back office," relaying information among Ukraine, the United States and European governments. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "I think he's really working hard and hopefully we'll get a solution," Stubb said. The interview came during an intense diplomatic week in New York focused heavily on the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in New York during UNGA week as Washington continued its effort to revive negotiations with Moscow. Zelenskyy said peace remained Ukraine's priority and thanked Trump for sending the two envoys to Kyiv after they had also held talks in Moscow. Zelenskyy was asked by Fox News Digital after the meeting about the possibility that Russia could invade or attack another European country in the near future. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "That's why the risk of offensive by drones, missiles or land operation is very high against other countries who are bordering Russia or Belarus," Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian leader argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin, unable to achieve his military objectives in Ukraine, could seek to create instability elsewhere in Europe to pressure Western governments into reducing their support for Kyiv. He pointed to drone incursions and disruptions affecting several European countries, arguing that Moscow is already attempting to intimidate European societies and test their response. Asked by Fox News Digital what European countries should do in response to the growing threat, Zelenskyy offered a direct answer. "Respond. Always respond. It's not about the war. If you don't respond, Russians, they will go further," he said. But Stubb struck a notably calmer tone when asked about Zelenskyy’s warnings that Russia could eventually attack other European countries, including Finland, which shares the longest border with Russia. "As commander-in-chief in Finland, I sit on all the relevant information and I just don't see a factual basis for it," Stubb said. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT That does not mean, he stressed, that Moscow has stopped targeting Europe. Stubb distinguished between the "kinetic" war Russia is fighting in Ukraine and what he described as a broader "hybrid" campaign in Europe, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. "We have to see this as a campaign," he said. "Russia tries to intimidate Europe, scare us and get into our heads." His prescription was characteristically Finnish: "cool, calm and collected, take a sauna and a nice bath and deal with it." Stubb said Finland, a country with a population of 5.6 million, can afford that attitude precisely because it has spent decades preparing for a potential threat from its eastern neighbor. "We are calm because we are prepared," he said. He pointed to Finland’s mandatory military service, reserve force, artillery, long-range capabilities and extensive network of civilian shelters. The Finnish Defence Forces puts Finland’s wartime military strength at 280,000 personnel, with additional reservists available if needed. That deterrent received another boost just days before Stubb traveled to New York. Finland is acquiring 64 F-35A fighter jets to replace its F/A-18 Hornet fleet under a procurement decision announced by the Finnish government. The first two F-35s intended for operations inside Finland arrived at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, according to a Finnish Defence Forces press release. "We have obligatory military service. I did mine, my son did his. We have women who do it voluntarily. We have over 60 F-18s. We just bought 64 F-35s, the two first of which arrived. We have long-range missiles, air, land and sea. We have the capability to mobilize 280,000 troops within days in a conflictual situation. On top of that, we have land mines. And we have the biggest artillery in Europe together with Poland… On top of that, we have civilian shelters for over 4.4 million people out of 5.6." FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT "We don't have them because we're worried about Sweden," Stubb joked of Finland’s military capabilities. "We have them because we see a security threat coming from Russia." He said that level of preparedness, combined with Finland’s NATO membership, makes a direct Russian attack unlikely. Finland became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, after abandoning its longstanding military non-alignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We feel that we're very prepared, and that gives us a strong enough … deterrent that we don't believe that Russia is going to test a country like Finland," Stubb said. "And of course the icing on the cake is that we are now security providers in the Alliance NATO." Stubb also used his Sept. 22 address to the U.N. General Assembly to advocate for continued support for Kyiv, calling the "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine "particularly close to my heart." He said the coalition was working toward a "just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the U.N. Charter." Stubb made additional news on Ukraine during UNGA week, when he urged SpaceX owner Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage so Ukrainian forces could use the satellite network in areas containing Russian ballistic missile launchers, including inside Russia. He argued that doing so could help Ukraine target launchers firing missiles at Ukrainian cities. Yet Ukraine was only one piece of what Stubb described as an increasingly interconnected global security crisis. WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? Asked about Trump’s call at the U.N. for countries to support efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, Stubb was unequivocal. "I agree, Iran should not obtain nuclear weapons," he told Fox News Digital, adding that Tehran should not use proxies or be able to produce missiles. Stubb also argued that the conflicts involving Russia and Iran can no longer be viewed in isolation, alleging that Moscow is providing intelligence to Tehran that Iran has used against U.S. military bases in the Gulf, while Iranian weapons have been supplied to Russia for use against Ukraine. "We're going in this merry-go-round where every bit of the conflict is linked to another," Stubb said. "The sooner we can end both, the better." Trump used his Sept. 22 U.N. General Assembly address to call for Iran's economic isolation and reiterate that Tehran should not obtain a nuclear weapon, while warning of further US military action if a peace agreement is not reached, according to Reuters. For Stubb, the proliferation of conflicts — from Ukraine and Iran to Gaza, Yemen and Sudan — is testing a diplomatic system already struggling to keep pace. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's not a zero-sum game," he said. "We have to deal with a multiplicity of conflicts right now, unfortunately." And for Trump, he added, that means "working around the clock."

articles.title: Andy Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
articles.summary: The prime minister told the BBC that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare".
articles.body:
Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election.

The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.

Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this.

Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's and died earlier this month .

While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded.

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work.

"There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush."

Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing.

Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse".

But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded.

When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high."

He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out".

Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there".

Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS."

He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus".

Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer.

On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament."

The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT.

Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide."

Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them.

He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget."

Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care.

He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy."

He told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms.

The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Burnham can show he is "serious about fixing care" by getting on with the cross-party talks that began in July.

He added: "This can't just be a series of No 10 headlines with no real action."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax.

"He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead."

Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy.

He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government.

It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died.

The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election.

At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000.

The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election.

articles.title: ‘No one is off the table’: Trump admin denies report of ICE pausing arrests of non-criminal illegal migrants
articles.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has dismissed a report that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers were instructed to stop
articles.body: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has dismissed a report that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers were instructed to stop arresting illegal migrants who have no criminal convictions or pending charges, saying “no one is off the table.”The denial came after The Daily Wire reported on September 26 that ICE officers across the US had been told to stop arresting “non-criminals” for the time being. Citing agency sources, the report said ICE officers would instead focus on undocumented migrants with criminal convictions or pending criminal charges.According to The Daily Wire, the reported guidance would also end so-called “collateral arrests”, in which ICE officers can detain other undocumented migrants encountered while pursuing a specific criminal target. Under the reported change, officers would arrest only the identified target.DHS rejects report of ICE arrest restrictionsDHS disputed the report on Saturday, sharing The Daily Wire report on X and calling the claim false.“This is false. No one is off the table,” DHS said. The department added that ICE would continue to arrest people who are unlawfully present in the US.“Anyone in our country illegally will be arrested and deported,” DHS said, while describing its current operations as a nationwide public-safety surge in sanctuary cities.The department said ICE officers were targeting undocumented migrants accused or convicted of serious crimes, including murder, rape, child sexual offences and gang-related crimes.The conflicting accounts leave it unclear whether any temporary internal guidance was issued to ICE officers or whether enforcement practices changed at specific locations.What The Daily Wire reportedThe Daily Wire said its sources described an apparent change in instructions to ICE officers that would limit arrests to undocumented migrants with criminal convictions or pending charges.The report quoted one ICE officer as saying the change was aimed at “calming things down” ahead of the US midterm elections. Another officer reportedly expressed opposition to the alleged instruction. The claims about the elections were based on anonymous sources and were not confirmed by DHS.Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin separately said he had spoken to nine ICE and DHS insiders who described “verbal guidance” being sent to ICE offices to avoid arrests of non-criminal migrants.Melugin said the guidance was later described as erroneous, with the situation attributed to a miscommunication over a policy of prioritising serious criminal offenders.The reported development comes amid a broader intensification of immigration enforcement under President Donald Trump. DHS has continued to announce arrests of illegal migrants with criminal convictions, while ICE recorded more than 50,000 arrests in August, according to data previously shared by DHS with The Daily Wire.For now, DHS clarifies that ICE has not been instructed to take non-criminal undocumented migrants off the table and says immigration arrests will continue nationwide.You use AI every day. articles.title: Moby Dick: When Hollywood came to Fishguard 70 years ago
articles.summary: The film, released 70 years ago, starred Gregory Peck as Captain Ahab and cost about $4m (£3m).
articles.body:
It is the seaside town that was transformed to Dylan Thomas' Llareggub in 1971, but Fishguard was also the backdrop for another iconic film.

Director John Huston chose the Pembrokeshire town as one of Moby Dick's locations, where the 19th-Century Nantucket whaling ship Pequod can be seen sailing.

The film, released 70 years ago in 1956, starred Gregory Peck as Captain Ahab and at the time was one of Hollywood's most expensive films, costing about $4m (£3m).

Although Fishguard itself does not feature as filming was done out at sea, locals still recall when Hollywood's stars took over the town.

Gareth Rees, who was 16 at the time, says there was "a buzz" in the area.

"It put Fishguard on the map for a long time," he said.

"My wife, Gina, her mother had a bed and breakfast, and she had three chauffeurs staying there. So there was a Rolls [Royce] and two Bentleys parked outside her house in Main Street. She said they were very good guests."

Gareth was a Sea Cadet, and his crew were challenged by some of the cast members to a rowing race.

"I can't remember who told me, 'you've got to come down the harbour', then I realised why we were down the harbour, for a race."

He said the Fishguard sea cadets won the race, with Gregory Peck as coxswain of the opposing team of Hollywood stars.

"He wasn't actually rowing, he had the easy job," he said.

"We were a good crew at the time, a good team. We were British champions and had been for about three or four years. Nobody could beat us at the time."

"He was a gentleman and everybody says that now, you'd never have thought that he was a big Hollywood star.

"I never thought I'd be this famous in 70 years time because I rowed against Gregory Peck."

Huw Lewis, also a part of the Fishguard Sea Cadets team and 16 at the time, accepted the award on behalf of the team, presented to him by Peck.

"I had no idea who on earth it was. They were very happy memories," he said.

Margaret Andrews, who grew up in Fishguard and was in sixth form during filming, got a summer job as a part of the makeup department based in the Fishguard Bay Hotel.

"I remember an aunt of mine told my parents 'I hear Margaret's got a holiday job and is based in the Bay Hotel with all those men'," she said.

"But eventually everybody accepted them and we got to see that they were just people."

She got the job through her boyfriend, who was a part of the team making Captain Ahab's famous scars for his face.

Margaret recalls seeing stars such as Peck on a daily basis and would sometimes get a lift home in one of the chauffeurs' Bentleys or Rolls-Royce.

"The makeup man in charge was very high up in Max Factor, he was the only one who was allowed to make up Gregory Peck."

As a teenager she said seeing stars like Peck was "very exciting". "He was such a very nice man."

"I'm very glad I experienced it. I didn't realise it at the time, it was an insight into another world."

To celebrate 70 years since the release of the film, its legacy is a major theme of this year's On Land's Edge Festival - an annual celebration of music, theatre, film and literature in north Pembrokeshire.

On Friday, the annual lantern parade featured an 8ft illuminated Moby Dick, as well as fish and ship lanterns made by pupils at Ysgol Bro Gwaun.

There was also an exhibition, The Making of Moby Dick: An Exhibition of Memories, at the local theatre, Theatr Gwaun.

Patrick Thomas, chair of trustees there, said: "There are still lots of people in the community here who remember the filming, who spent time with Gregory Peck, John Huston and Bernard Miles. We were able to bring those memories back to life and put them on display."

articles.title: South Korea's KF-21 Boramae is flying, AMCA still on paper: The stark fighter-jet race India cannot afford to lose
articles.summary: South Korea and India are both developing twin-engine fifth-generation fighter jets, but as of September 26, 2026, the two programmes could not be at more
articles.body: South Korea and India are both developing twin-engine fifth-generation fighter jets, but as of September 26, 2026, the two programmes could not be at more different points on the development curve.The Republic of Korea Air Force has already taken delivery of its first production KF-21 Boramae, while India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) is still waiting for the industry partner that will build its first prototypes to be finalised. The contrast is not just about timelines. It also reflects two fundamentally different philosophies for developing a next-generation fighter.Korea inducts the BoramaeThe KF-21 programme formally began in December 2015. Korea Aerospace Industries rolled out the first prototype in April 2021, and it made its maiden flight in July 2022. Over the following years, six prototypes completed more than 1,600 test sorties across roughly 13,000 test conditions, covering weapons trials, aerial refuelling, high-angle-of-attack manoeuvres and radar testing.The flight-test campaign concluded in January 2026. The aircraft received final approvals in May, secured type certification in June, and the system development phase was formally closed the following month.On September 22, the first production KF-21 was handed over to the South Korean Air Force at Yecheon Air Base. The aircraft was escorted by Korean-developed jets, including the FA-50, TA-50 and T-50. Seoul plans to formally declare the KF-21 operational in the second half of 2027.But the KF-21 entering service today is not the final version envisioned by the South Korean Air Force. Seoul has deliberately structured the programme around successive capability blocks.Block I, the version now being delivered, is a 4.5-generation aircraft focused primarily on air-to-air combat. The first 40 aircraft will be delivered in this configuration. Block II will add air-to-ground capabilities, and South Korea has brought forward the timeline for their integration. The Defence Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) announced in August that these weapons would begin arriving in stages in the first half of 2027, rather than being integrated in bulk only by the end of 2028.The broader plan calls for 120 KF-21s. The first 40 will focus on air superiority, while the remaining 80 are planned to have air-to-ground and anti-ship capabilities by 2032.South Korea has also outlined a longer-term evolution towards a full fifth-generation configuration, with improved stealth characteristics and, eventually, sixth-generation features such as an internal weapons bay, which would reduce radar signature and improve aerodynamics, along with AI-assisted systems and manned-unmanned teaming. These, however, remain future ambitions rather than capabilities of the aircraft entering service today.Long road for AMCA India's AMCA has been conceived differently from the outset. Rather than starting with a 4.5-generation aircraft and building up its capabilities, the AMCA is being designed from the ground up as a fifth-generation stealth fighter, with low observability and internal weapons carriage central to its architecture.Two variants are planned. The AMCA Mk1 will be powered by the GE F414 engine, while the more advanced Mk2 is expected to use a higher-thrust indigenous engine being developed with foreign collaboration. This has been envisaged from the outset as the aircraft's long-term growth path, rather than simply as a future weapons upgrade.The programme received a major institutional boost in 2024, when the Cabinet Committee on Security cleared the Full Scale Engineering Development (FSED) phase at a cost of roughly Rs 15,000 crore for five flying prototypes.In May 2025, the defence ministry approved a model under which the Aeronautical Development Agency would execute the programme jointly with a private industry partner. This opened prototype construction to the private sector for the first time in a major Indian fighter programme.By May 2026, the ministry had issued a request for proposals to three shortlisted contenders: Tata Advanced Systems, an L&T-BEL-Dynamatic consortium, and a Bharat Forge-BEML-Data Patterns grouping. The deadline for submitting bids has since been extended twice.As things stand, India has not yet reached the point South Korea had already crossed in 2021, when the first KF-21 prototype rolled out of the factory.The bidding deadline for the AMCA industry partner, originally set for late July, has now been extended to the end of September, with bids scheduled to be opened the following day. The winning company will have to build five prototypes and one structural test specimen, achieve a maiden flight within 30 months of signing the contract, and complete an 84-month, seven-year programme involving 1,800 test sorties before series production can begin.Placed side by side, the timelines tell their own story. South Korea moved from the formal launch of the KF-21 programme in December 2015 to prototype rollout in less than six years. The aircraft flew for the first time the following year and, roughly a decade after the programme began, a production aircraft has already been handed over to the air force.India, by contrast, is still selecting the company that will build its first AMCA prototype. Its equivalent milestones, including first flight, certification and induction, therefore remain years away and will depend heavily on when the production contract is finally signed.Earlier projections had pointed to an AMCA prototype rollout in late 2026 or early 2027 and induction by 2034. With the industry-partner selection itself now delayed, however, those timelines increasingly look aspirational.IAF's big falling numbers worryIndia faces a two-front threat from Pakistan and China, with the risk of collusive action between them, making a whole-of-government strategy involving diplomacy, economic leverage, alliances and credible military deterrence essential. Air power remains central to this calculus, and the immediate priority is building up IAF numbers quickly. This context is key to assessing the upcoming Rafale deal. Delays in the AMCA programme could eventually force New Delhi to choose between competing priorities, making it critical that the government designates AMCA a mission of national importance to ensure timely delivery. Meanwhile, the IAF's dangerously dwindling fleet need urgent augmentation. It needs MRFA of at least 4/4.5 generation; ideally that should have been LCA Mk1a and Mk2. However, the delay forces an unpleasant choice- import.The comparison matters for reasons beyond admiration or anxiety about another country's fighter programme. It comes at a time when the Indian Air Force's fighter squadron strength has fallen to 29, well below its sanctioned strength of 42, largely following the retirement of the MiG-21 fleet last September.That shortfall of roughly 13 squadrons is unlikely to disappear soon. The Jaguar fleet, which still numbers around 120 aircraft across six squadrons, will eventually need replacement even as DARIN III upgrades are expected to keep the aircraft flying until around 2035.The Tejas Mk2, which was once expected to help plug the gap with a first flight in 2026, has also slipped, with recent estimates now pointing to 2027.India is looking further ahead as well. The defence ministry is exploring possible participation in the French-led Future Combat Air System (FCAS) for a future sixth-generation fighter, an option it discussed with the parliamentary committee on defence.But that programme itself remains in flux. France and Germany parted ways on their joint crewed-fighter effort earlier this year, although they are continuing cooperation on the combat cloud. India's sixth-generation discussions are therefore taking place at an even earlier and more uncertain stage than the AMCA programme.India is also a dialogue partner in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), the sixth-generation fighter effort being developed jointly by the UK, Japan and Italy.The picture is ultimately one of two very different approaches to fighter development.South Korea chose to get a workable, upgradeable aircraft into the hands of its air force relatively quickly and build its capabilities over successive blocks. India is betting on a more ambitious leap directly to fifth-generation stealth.That ambition, however, comes with a longer runway. And every month spent finalising an industry partner is another month before the IAF gets its first AMCA prototype, while the service continues to operate with a fighter fleet well below its authorised strength.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi PWD Minister Parvesh Verma was seen allegedly slapping a man during a road inspection in Tilak Nagar on Sunday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi PWD Minister Parvesh Verma was seen allegedly slapping a man during a road inspection in Tilak Nagar on Sunday.In the video shared by AAP leaders, Verma can be seen pulling down the man's mobile phone with his left hand and slapping him across the face with his right hand.The man, identified as Saheb, then appears to confront the minister before a security guard steps between them. Several people can be seen gathered around the two."Oye maar kaise raha hai (How are you hitting)," a man can be heard saying in the video.The incident took place while Verma was inspecting a road in the area.Speaking to ANI, Saheb said he handles social media activities for the local MLA and had come to the spot after the PWD department called them to inspect the condition of the road."I showed him how the road surface was breaking apart. When this was pointed out, the Minister couldn't handle it; he raised his hand against me, and his associates threatened to kill me," he said.Saheb alleged that police personnel were present when the incident took place."He must apologise, and whatever disciplinary action is required - such as suspension - should be taken," Saheb said, adding that there was video evidence of the incident."We aren't just making claims; there is video evidence of everything. Action must be taken. We have lodged an FIR and will pursue further action," he said.AAP MLA Jarnail Singh, who represents Tilak Nagar, also shared a video of the incident and accused Verma of assaulting the man who was recording the proceedings.Singh said he had accompanied Verma during the road inspection and pointed out portions of the road where the surface was coming off. He alleged that instead of taking action over the road's condition, Verma slapped the person recording the incident.Singh also alleged that the SHO of Vikaspuri police station was present when the incident occurred and accused the officer of helping the minister leave the spot."We have called the emergency number - 112 - to report this," Singh said in the video.Singh said he would remain at the spot until an FIR was registered and Verma was arrested. He also called on the Delhi Police Commissioner to take action against the minister under the law.Former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also shared Singh's video and called for Verma's arrest.Parvesh Verma reveals the 'truth behind' videoVerma, responding to the video, said people should know the "truth behind" what he described as a video being circulated by the Aam Aadmi Party.He alleged that road construction work had been underway on the Vikaspuri Ring Road for several days and claimed that Jarnail Singh had been pressuring PWD engineers to introduce him to the contractor and arrange a commission for him.Verma said a PWD engineer had lodged a complaint at a police station and was getting an FIR registered.He further alleged that Singh would visit the site after roadwork was completed at night, tear up the newly laid road and record videos alleging corruption because he had not received a commission.Verma said he had stopped at the site on Sunday to inspect the road and found that the work was progressing well. articles.title: Our Friends in the North play still relevant - Peter Flannery
articles.summary: Peter Flannery says a new stage version of the classic TV show will resonate with modern audiences.
articles.body:
The writer of acclaimed 1990s BBC TV drama Our Friends in the North has said a new stage version will resonate with modern audiences, even if he had once thought its themes would become irrelevant.

Peter Flannery, who was born and raised in Jarrow, said he had hoped the corruption and poverty the original show explored in the North East would fade away.

But in an interview ahead of a new stage adaptation in Newcastle, he said he was expecting the 21st Century audience to recognise the same problems today.

"If you asked me 30 years ago, would things be as bad as they are now, I'd probably have said no. I'd have said things are sure to get better and we would do something about inequality, corruption, greed, deprivation in pockets of the UK."

"So the fact it's got worse wasn't me being prescient. I didn't know it was going to get worse, it just has."

Flannery has adapted two episodes from the original nine-part series into a play that will open at Newcastle's Theatre Royal on 15 October.

It covers the years between Margaret Thatcher becoming prime minister in 1979 and the miners' strike of 1984, showing the impact of events on "friends" Nicky, Mary, Geordie and Tosker – and the North East.

Flannery added: "I wish, in my political heart, it was all now irrelevant. But with my vanity and my desire to be listened to as a writer, I do feel validated."

But he said as well as exploring problems the drama offered hope.

"Through the characters, it shows the enduring nature of love and friendship, and that, even though all this stuff is going on, people survive."

The TV series launched the careers of the four main actors, Daniel Craig, Christopher Eccleston, Gina McKee and Mark Strong.

And the new stage play also features a cast that is hoping it will have an impact on their futures as well as the audience.

Ryan Nolan, 30, from Newcastle, was born in the week the TV series first aired. He is Nicky Hutchinson, the role originally played by Christopher Eccleston.

He said: "I've worked as an actor for 10 years, but I've never had more people want to talk to me since being cast. Saying they're coming to see it, saying they love the original, saying they can't wait to see what I do with it.

But Scott Turnbull, 45, from Stockton, who plays Geordie, is not expecting his career to follow the path of original cast member Daniel Craig, who ended up as a buff James Bond, emerging from the sea when he debuted in the role in Casino Royale.

"What I would say is don't expect me to enter Act Two in a pair of Speedos looking absolutely ripped. I think the bird on the James Bond ticket might have already flown!"

The cast agree that the drama will appeal to both fans of the original and audiences encountering it for the first time.

Sam Neale, 41, from Newcastle, who plays Mary said: "At the centre of it you've got inadequate social housing, mistrust of the police and mass unemployment.

"All issues we are still dealing with. If younger audiences are coming in and have no point of reference to the miners' strike, they will relate to and understand a lack of opportunity or the difficulty getting a house."

And Jack Robertson, from Whitley Bay, who plays Tosker said it will also give younger audiences an insight into how the region was impacted by the 1980s.

"A lot of what we are doing is showing the loss of community back in those days. Even if you knew jobs were under threat, there was still this sense of people knowing each other and that family feel.

"That's such a highlight of the show and by virtue of comparison, it shows how divided we are now."

Flannery is not taking part in rehearsals but is looking forward to seeing it on stage, though he did have doubts about returning to Our Friends in the North.

"When I see it I think I'll have moments of elation and moments of thinking why did you do this Peter, why didn't you just stop?

"But actually I think it will be a success. And I hope it will tour the country next."

Our Friends in the North – The Thatcher Years runs at Newcastle's Theatre Royal between 15 and 24 October.

articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: Three abortions and eight decades later, this woman says feminism 'failed' her
articles.summary: Candy Thompson says feminism pitted women against men, children, and God, leading to three abortions before she returned to her Christian faith.
articles.body: Octogenarian Candy Thompson, who says she left her Christian faith after embracing feminism and later had three abortions during her first marriage, eventually returned to Christianity and said feminism "failed" her. "The feminists pitted [women] against men, they pitted us against having children … It belittled who we were in the home and [as] mothers, and it belittled who we were as just women in a marriage," Thompson told Fox News Digital. "When it pitted us against God even … then that's what really led to what happened to me," she continued. DEPROGRAMMED: THE 'RADICAL PERSPECTIVE CHANGE' THAT LED THIS TRANSGENDER ATHEIST TO JESUS Thompson, who attended the University of North Carolina in the 1960s, said learning about feminism while in college helped lead her away from her Christian values. "[Those values] didn't seem to answer the questions that I was asking. And then I heard about feminism, and that was in the culture … It sounded good because it was about equality," she added. "I had a really, really traumatic experience between my junior and senior year. I had a miscarriage in the college dorm … Instead of going to my parents, instead of going back to God … I just went right on with what I had been doing. articles.title: Prime Minister Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow
articles.summary: Andy Burnham said he would wait for the results of a consultation on a scheme estimated to cost £33bn
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs a third runway at Heathrow after it emerged that the expansion of the London airport could be delayed by up to four years.

Burnham - who, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, opposed the project - told Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: "I think principally, it's a matter for London and Londoners."

He added: "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation."

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had championed the runway to boost the economy, with a schedule to open by 2035 but Heathrow indicated on Saturday it may not be operational before 2039.

As Manchester's mayor, Burnham had been against the project over concerns that it would delay investment in transport for the north. When he took office, he said he was "open-minded" about the scheme.

As he prepared for his first annual Labour Party conference as prime minister, Burnham said: "There's a consultion but there are different views and you have to take those views seriously in coming to a decision."

In response, Heathrow said: "We agree with the prime minister that local voices must be heard. We know from consistent polling over the last decade that communities support our plans for expansion and support is only growing over time."

The project, estimated to cost £33bn, has attracted opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups as well as Mayor of London Sadiq Khan.

A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers and rerouting a section of the M25 motorway through a tunnel.

But it is estimated it would create 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the UK economy.

The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000, or nearly 2,000 a day on average.

A new runway has been backed by the unions Unite and the GMB.

Sharon Graham, Unite's general secretary said: "A third runway at Heathrow is essential and we need to get going with it.

"This is more than just infrastructure. It's about investing in the workforce, securing the future of good, unionised jobs and a guaranteed market for UK steel."

Earlier this weekend, Heathrow conceded that meeting the original deadline would be increasingly difficult without further steps to simplify the planning process.

It said it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".

The Department for Transport said the timeline had "always been ambitious" and it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.

articles.title: Favourite trees sought for Guernsey art project
articles.summary: People have been invited to share pictures of their favourite trees as part of a new art project.
articles.body:
People have been asked to name their favourite trees in Guernsey as part of new art installation.

As part of its forthcoming exhibition Guernsey's Iconic Trees, Art for Guernsey has invited people to send in photographs of trees that may have personal significance to them.

It said, in addition to the photos, people were being encouraged to send a close-up photograph of one of its leaves and the story behind it.

Once the submissions had been received, it said French artist Anna van der Hoek would create an original linocut of the tree, to be added to a growing leporello - an accordion-like, never-ending artist's book.

Art for Guernsey said people could add their tree to the project themselves by using a leaf stamp, so the work could continue to grow as more people contributed to it.

It said all submissions needed to be sent by 4 October.

articles.title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope, during Lourdes visit
articles.summary: Pope Leo spoke to bishops before leading a service attended by thousands of worshippers in France.
articles.body:
Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors.

The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.

A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.

The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later.

Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.

"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."

The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.

The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.

Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.

On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.

During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".

The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech , describing them as "today's Church".

"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.

The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.

But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.

Later on Sunday the Pope will meet staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, before taking part in a torchlight procession in the evening.

It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic church in May 2025.

Pope's have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots.

articles.title: College football week 4 contenders, pretenders: Texas survives, Michigan's karma and coaches are sweating
articles.summary: Iowa stunned Michigan on a last-second touchdown, and LSU's Lane Kiffin sent Texas A&M fans into panic mode on a wild college football Saturday.
articles.body: KNOXVILLE, TN - It only took four weeks of action to immerse ourselves in the madness of college football, with upsets and teams already up against the ropes heading into the month of October. Are schools already looking to make changes at the head coaching position? Sure, and some leaders might end up making the decision pretty easy for their bosses. But what we witnessed on Saturday will go down as one of the wildest weekends of this early season, and there will be ramifications. ARCH MANNING REVELS IN CIGAR SMOKE: TEXAS LEAVES NEYLAND WITH WIN—AND A WARNING FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL Heck, Texas led Tennessee by ten points late in the fourth quarter, but had to withstand a last minute drive by the Vols to get out of Knoxville with the win. There wasn’t even a touchdown pass thrown by Arch Manning on Saturday, but the defense ended up with over ten sacks on Vols quarterback Faizon Brandon, in what felt like a Will Muschamp defensive revival. We're only getting started on this wild weekend in college football. Oregon lost quarterback Dante Moore to a head injury in the first half, thanks to a dirty hit. But, that did not end their hopes of beating USC. Two weeks after losing to Oklahoma State, the Ducks rolled into Southern Cal and once again left Trojan fans wondering when Lincoln Riley was going to win a few meaningful games. We don't know when Moore will return, but backup Dylan Raiola took the reigns on Saturday night and never looked back. Throwing for over 280 yards against USC, this might be the start of Raiola's redemption tour, at least until Dante Moore returns. But, a massive 41-27 win for the Ducks have put their season back on track, while USC fans are left wondering what else Lincoln Riley feels like putting them through. Who would of thought before the season started that Oklahoma would already be regretting that contract extension for Brent Venables. But just four games into the 2026 season, the Sooners have a major problem on their hands, thanks in part to the 41-13 drumming by the Georgia Bulldogs on Saturday afternoon in Athens. Not a trap, Florida earned Ole Miss' respect. Beamer in trouble. Hey, Kamario Taylor Oh, and if you were wondering whether Ole Miss was walking into a trap this week in Gainesville after defeating LSU last weekend, I think that would be disrespecting what Jon Sumrall is doing with the Florida Gators. A 52-28 loss on the road brought the Rebels back down to reality, with Pete Golding having to regroup his team this week after a rollercoaster two-week stretch. But make no mistake about it, the Florida Gators look nothing like the team we witnessed during the Billy Napier era. FLORIDA DROPS IMPRESSIVE OFFENSIVE PERFORMANCE TO PULL OFF MASSIVE WIN OVER NO. 4 OLE MISS And, speaking of teams we thought could get things back on track in 2026, South Carolina has itself a major problem moving forward under head coach Shane Beamer. Not only were they beaten 49-18 by Alabama, the Gamecocks feel like a rudderless ship, with such high expectations for quarterback LaNorris Sellers before the season began. Now? The Gamecocks lost their seventh-straight SEC game, and it doesn’t look any better moving forward. Well, this is only going to make things worse in Columbia for Beamer, who had spent a good chunk of money to keep a number of stars from hitting the portal, like Dylan Stewart. Is Kamario Taylor going to end up being the catalyst that brings Mississippi State back to college football relevance? Well, he already has, and looks darn good in the process. The 24th ranked Bulldogs defeated No. 19 Missouri, winning their first ranked game in over a decade, with Taylor passing for over 350 yards on the night. Look out, Alabama. The Bulldogs are waiting next week in Starkville. \ Karma finally comes calling for Michigan. LSU sends Texas A&M fans into panic mode Yes, you read that right. An Iowa Hawkeyes touchdown with only one second left on the clock left Michigan fans stunned, probably the same way Western Michigan fans felt during the week-one controversy that allowed the Wolverines to escape with a win. Three weeks later, it was Kirk Ferentz who delivered the karma like a Taylor Swift single, which had college football fans outside of the state chuckling I'd imagine. No, this looks nothing like a team that should be paying its quarterback Bryce Underwood over $3 million per season. In reality, this feels like a squad headed for a December bowl game, and nowhere near the Big Ten championship. At this point, maybe it would be wise for Michigan fans to start preparing for the Ohio State game to end the season, and not get their hopes up every weekend. That win against Oklahoma also looks even worse by the week. So, you thought Lane Kiffin would just go quiet into the night after losing to his former team last week in Oxford? Umm, no. Not only did LSU take out their frustration on Texas A&M, but they made it look easy in the 38-6 win. Sam Leavitt carved up the Aggies secondary, while Kiffin found himself running down the sidelines celebrating a fourth-down trick play that turned into a touchdown. Simply put, the Tigers made Mike Elko's squad look like a mediocre SEC team without much hope moving forward. We should probably go ahead and count the Aggies out of making the College Football Playoff, while LSU looks to have gotten the 'Lane Train' back on the tracks in Baton Rouge. What in the world moments on Saturday... Can someone explain to me how Louisville could lose at home to Wake Forest 30-27, with this squad battling for 'surprise' team of the season out of the ACC? Well, that went up in smoke inside their own stadium. Oh, and how could we not mention the job Luke Fickell did on Saturday, leading his Wisconsin Badgers into Happy Valley and leaving with the 24-20 win that left folks in State College shocked. People forget that Fickell didn’t just wake up and turn into a bad coach. He just hasn’t had the necessary resources in Madison. He still might not have everything he needs to rebuild the Wisconsin football team, but they darn sure made Penn State pay for potentially looking past the Badgers. Week four of the college football season delivered, which will setup a wild start to the month of October. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Expect anything less?

articles.title: Tamil Nadu govt rolls back law and order department’s RTI exemption amid backlash
articles.summary: The Tamil Nadu government on Sunday withdrew its notification exempting the Public (Law and Order) Department from the Right to Information Act, hours
articles.body: The Tamil Nadu government on Sunday withdrew its notification exempting the Public (Law and Order) Department from the Right to Information Act, hours after issuing the Gazette notification that classified the department as an "Intelligence and Security Organisation".The rollback came after the move drew criticism from political leaders, including Congress's Karti P Chidambaram and BJP's Tamilisai Soundararajan. The government, however, did not publicly cite a specific reason for issuing the exemption or explain why it was withdrawn. An official communication later confirmed that the order issued under Section 24(4) of the RTI Act had been rescinded, reported ANI.What was the notification?The original notification, issued by the Human Resources Management Department and published in the state Gazette, used the power available to state governments under Section 24(4) of the RTI Act. The provision allowed a state government to notify an organisation established by it as an intelligence or security organisation, thereby taking it outside the normal scope of the RTI Act.Tamil Nadu's notification designated its Public (Law and Order) Department as such an organisation. Had it remained in force, routine RTI access to a broad range of records held by the department would have been restricted.The records covered included information relating to communal and caste clashes, political agitations, police action and custody, deaths of prisoners, police firing, inquiries into law-and-order incidents and requests for withdrawal of cases arising from political or communal tensions.The exemption was not absolute. Section 24 specifically preserves access to information relating to allegations of corruption and human-rights violations, subject to the procedure prescribed under the Act.The notification itself invoked Section 24(4) and classified the department as an intelligence and security organisation. The government has not, in the material available publicly gave a detailed explanation for why the Public (Law and Order) Department was brought under this provision.The department handles sensitive law-and-order and policing-related matters, which appears to be the basis on which the exemption was framed. But that is distinct from saying that the government officially justified the move on a particular security ground. The notification, as reported, simply exercised the statutory power under Section 24(4).The backlashThe proposed exemption would have affected access to records concerning issues such as police firing, custodial deaths, torture, communal and caste clashes and politically sensitive cases, prompting criticism that the move could reduce transparency.Karti Chidambaram initially criticised the decision, saying it "does not set a good precedent" and recalling that the RTI Act was enacted by the UPA government to strengthen democratic accountability."The Law and Order Department handles crucial matters such as examining inquiry reports on police firing, custodial deaths, torture, and deaths of remand prisoners, security-related detention cases, communal and caste clash reports, requests for withdrawal of politically sensitive cases and matters relating to sanction of prosecution for defamatory articles, news items, and speeches. This crucial information is now being shielded from the public. Such rollbacks are not in line with transparent governance. RTI must be expanded, not restricted," Chidambaram posted on X.After the government withdrew the notification, he welcomed the decision, saying: "My unsolicited & friendly advice to the TVK Government & CMO Tamil Nadu — don't let bureaucrats set the tone, tenor & direction of the administration."BJP's Tamilisai Soundararajan also criticised the original notification, saying: "So they are afraid of meeting the press, they are afraid of meeting the people, and they are afraid of the legal procedures. If you are free and fair, why are you afraid of RTI?" She called the move "undemocratic" and said it should be "highly condemned."With the withdrawal of the notification, the Public (Law and Order) Department is no longer covered by the newly created exemption.The RTI Act, 2005, establishes a legal framework for citizens to access information held by public authorities, subject to exemptions specified in the law.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Floods and landslides kill at least 56 people in India, 12 in Nepal
articles.summary: Authorities report increasing death toll over three days as rivers rise above danger levels in parts of both countries.
articles.body:
Heavy rainfall has triggered floods and landslides that have killed at least 56 people in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh in recent days while 12 people have been reported dead in neighbouring Nepal.

Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod, Uttar Pradesh’s relief commissioner, said on Sunday that India’s most populous state had registered 66.5mm (2.6 inches) of rain from Friday to Sunday morning, compared with a normal 7.6mm (a quarter of an inch) for the period.

The deaths, in addition to 46 injuries, were reported during a spell of “exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh”, according to the commissioner’s office.

More than 1,000 houses were damaged after “a depression over the Bay of Bengal moved inland and intensified rainfall across the region,” it added.

Home to more than 240 million people, Uttar Pradesh is frequently hit by rain and thunderstorms during the annual monsoon season from June to September.

In India’s eastern state of Odisha, more than 70,000 people living in low-lying areas were evacuated after rivers rose due to heavy downpours, the NDTV news network reported. The rains have damaged bridges and culverts, forcing officials to shut down Devkund, a popular tourist spot in the state.

Separately, India’s Central Water Commission said 30 river-monitoring stations across seven states were in a “severe situation”. Major rivers that flow through India, including the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi, Bagmati and Narmada, had risen above danger levels.

In Nepal, where a devastating flood in late August killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing, a new wave of flooding and landslides has killed at least 12 people since Thursday, according to officials, with several others missing.

Authorities warned of possible flash floods in 49 of the country’s 77 districts, with more than half facing high flooding or flash-flooding risks as water levels in major rivers and tributaries continued to rise.

Power supplies have been disrupted in the Manang, Mustang, Myagdi and Baglung districts, with authorities working to ⁠restore electricity, officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said.

Flooding of the Rahuganga River damaged the structure and transmission-line towers of a 40-megawatt hydropower project, Water Resources and Energy ⁠Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said.

Shanti Mahat, a spokesperson for the National ⁠Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Rasuwa and Nuwakot, areas hit by ⁠last month’s deadly floods, should remain “alert” but were not currently considered high-risk areas.

articles.summary: In 1988, Ohio lawyer Neil McKown signed a deal to buy 155 acres of overgrown, run-down land in Shelby.
articles.body: In 1988, Ohio lawyer Neil McKown signed a deal to buy 155 acres of overgrown, run-down land in Shelby. When he got home that evening, he asked his family to get into the car to see what he had just bought. His wife, Pamela, was not impressed by the property. She thought it was an eyesore. But that quiet, impulsive purchase began a decades-long effort to care for the land. Thirty-eight years later, the McKown family manages nearly 500 acres in Richland County, raising row crops, alfalfa, hay, and cattle. Their work to improve soil health, manage water, and care for the woods has earned them the Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award, according to Farm Progress.Escape from the courtroomNeil McKown spent years practicing law with his father. He and his family lived in a suburban home on seven acres. Over time, the pressure of legal work began to wear on him. He tried hobbies such as trap shooting and golf to relax. But people often approached him during his free time to ask for legal advice. "I needed to be by myself, without the computer, email, phone or people," Neil told Farm Progress editor Jennifer Kiel. "I wanted to be left alone with my thoughts." Going back to his rural roots seemed like the right choice. He had grown up five miles from where the family farm is today and had worked summer jobs on nearby farms. But moving into farming full time was still a major learning experience. When he planted his first soybean crop in 1990, three neighboring farmers stopped to look at his grain drill. They were concerned that he did not know what he was doing. Neil said he still laughs when he thinks about those early days, but the family kept going.Turning forced fun into family progressThe original property had about 80 tillable acres. The rest was made up of overgrown woods and pasture. Improving the neglected land became a family project for Neil, Pamela, and their young children, Sam and Lauren. To improve the timber stands, the family spent Sunday afternoons clearing grapevines through a conservation district cost-share program. "We'd work until noon, 1 o'clock, and build a fire and have weenie roasts," Neil told Farm Progress. "We called it forced fun." He let the children keep whatever cost-share money they earned from the work. Fixing the farm's drainage was just as difficult. The farm sits in a prehistoric lake basin with heavy, silty soil and only one working drainage outlet. Instead of depending on outside contractors, the McKowns worked with a neighbor to the south to dig a ditch that connected with an existing drainage system. Over five years, they added tile drainage across the fields and planted 30-foot grass buffer strips along the ditch banks to help protect water quality. "A lot of things that we've done, we've just gone out and done, and really haven't sought a whole lot of outside help or resources," Neil told Farm Progress. "We just do what's right."Choosing trees over cashThe family grew its land holdings as nearby properties went up for sale. In the mid-1990s, they added cattle and hay equipment. By age 14, Sam McKown was doing custom hay work for neighboring farms. Today, managing the woods is still a major part of the family's conservation work. Working with a former Ohio State forester, Neil has focused on improving the forest over the long term instead of making quick money from it. The forester told him that a heavy timber harvest could bring in between $400,000 and $500,000. Neil turned down the money. "I'd rather see the woods," he said, explaining that his main goal was to improve the timber stand. The family has also removed invasive burning bush, set up an apiary, maintained a farm pond, and hosted educational days for local school children. Students have learned about vernal pools, wildlife, glaciers, and the history of the land.Handing over the reinsSam McKown, now 43, has become the main manager of the farm's daily work. He puts much of his time into producing high-quality hay. About 90 percent of his hay is sold to horse owners and cattle producers. He also manages 15 head of beef cattle. To build his own place in farming, Sam bought another 130 acres near Ontario, Ohio. He grows alfalfa and row crops there. He also placed 40 acres into a 15-year Conservation Reserve Program reforestation effort. His sister, Lauren, chose law and healthcare policy and works in Columbus. Sam also defended farmers against criticism over environmental problems. "I think farmers get a bad rap," Sam told Farm Progress. "Most people involved in agriculture that own land, that farmland — it's a generational thing, and they're doing their best to manage profit while protecting the environment." For Pamela, the doubts she had in the early days have turned into an appreciation for the quiet life the family created from that sudden land purchase. "My friends see this as work," Pamela said. "But it's something we enjoy. I love being out here. I find it peaceful."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Four American tourists among 6 killed after explosion levels building near Athens’ Acropolis
articles.summary: A suspected gas leak caused an explosions that leveled a residential building in Athens' Plaka district near the Acropolis, killing four American tourists and two residents.
articles.body: Four American tourists were among six people killed in Greece when a devastating explosion leveled a residential building near Athens’ famed Acropolis, according to officials. The four Americans — two men and two women believed to be two couples — were staying in the two-story building in the historic Plaka district, the historic neighborhood at the foot of the Acropolis and close to some of Athens’ most heavily visited landmarks, when the blast struck Friday. The two couples had been expected to catch a flight from Athens airport at 3 p.m. Friday but never showed up, a police source told Reuters. Documents and belongings recovered with the four victims indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media. AMERICAN TOURISTS STABBED OUTSIDE ATHENS' ACROPOLIS AS POLICE DETAIN SUSPECT IN APPARENT RANDOM ATTACK U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle mourned the victims in a post on X. "I am deeply saddened to learn of the death of four American citizens in yesterday’s explosion in central Athens," Guilfoyle wrote. Emergency crews searching through the rubble recovered six bodies from the collapsed building Saturday, authorities said. Firefighters had been searching for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists staying in another as crews painstakingly removed debris, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said in a televised briefing. EXPLOSION NEAR GERMAN TRAIN STATION INJURES 2 UKRAINIAN CITIZENS The explosion was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Authorities were investigating the cause after reports of a gas smell in the area. The powerful blast destroyed the building and damaged nearby homes, shops and vehicles, sending rubble and shattered glass as far as three blocks away, Reuters reported. Video from the scene showed debris strewn across the street and parked cars crushed beneath falling rubble. The destroyed building was reduced to twisted metal, broken tiles and concrete, with clothing and household belongings scattered among the wreckage. The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, while crews also used cameras and sensors to comb through the debris. Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, according to the fire department. Resident Andreas Martzaklis told the Associated Press that all those rescued from the neighboring building were tourists. articles.title: Nepal: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
articles.summary: The Nepali team was preparing to take overseas climbers up the Himlung Himal peak.
articles.body:
At least 10 Nepalese climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition in the Himalayas are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp on Sunday morning.

The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck.

Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.

Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing."

The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.

Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.

Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.

The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan , including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja.

Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.

It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.

More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.

articles.title: Swiss voters set to reject tighter neutrality rules in referendum
articles.summary: About 71 percent of voters oppose initiative to impose stricter limits on neutrality, projection suggests.
articles.body:
Swiss voters appear to have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to impose stricter constitutional limits on the country’s longstanding neutrality.

About 71 percent voted against the initiative in a referendum on Sunday, according to a projection by the polling institute GFS Bern for the Swiss public broadcaster SRG.

The result would preserve the government’s ability to impose sanctions and cooperate with NATO , the transatlantic military alliance whose members include most of Switzerland ’s larger neighbours, rather than lock those choices into a narrower constitutional definition of neutrality.

The initiative sought to define Swiss neutrality as “perpetual and armed”.

It would have barred Switzerland from joining or cooperating with military and defence alliances unless the country was under attack or an attack was imminent while allowing sanctions against states at war only when approved by the United Nations Security Council.

Pro Switzerland, a group that campaigns for national sovereignty, organised the initiative, which was backed by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP), Switzerland’s largest party.

Supporters argued that joining European Union sanctions against Russia and expanding security cooperation with NATO had weakened the country’s traditional neutral role.

The Swiss government, parliament and nearly all major parties opposed the proposal, saying it would leave the country less able to respond to international crises.

SRG said it projected about 29 percent support for the initiative.

The argument over neutrality sharpened after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 .

Switzerland largely adopted EU sanctions against Moscow, prompting criticism from Russia and from supporters of stricter neutrality, who said the Swiss government was taking sides.

Switzerland has been internationally recognised as neutral since 1815, and neutrality has formed part of its federal constitutional framework since 1848.

Current policy still allows the country to cooperate with other states on security and to join sanctions while remaining outside military alliances.

The vote, therefore, centred less on whether Switzerland should remain neutral than on how much freedom its government should retain in applying that principle as Europe’s security environment changes.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia arrests over 13,600 residency, labour law violators in week-long crackdown
articles.summary: Saudi authorities have arrested 13,628 individuals for breaking residency, border security, and labor laws during a week of inspections. Ethiopian nationals made up the majority of those arrested. The Ministry of Interior warns of severe penalties for those assisting illegal entrants.
articles.body: Saudi authorities arrested 13,628 people for violating residency, border security and labour laws during a week of nationwide inspections, the Ministry of Interior said on Saturday, Saudi Gazette reported.The arrests were made between September 17 and September 23 during joint inspections conducted by security forces in cooperation with relevant government agencies.Of those arrested, 6,593 were found to have violated the Residency Law, while 3,531 had breached the Border Security Law and 3,504 had violated the Labour Law.Authorities also arrested 1,197 people while they were attempting to cross the border into Saudi Arabia illegally. Ethiopian nationals accounted for 63% of those arrested, while 36% were Yemeni nationals. The remaining 1% belonged to other nationalities.Another 27 people were arrested while attempting to leave the country illegally.During the same period, authorities deported 12,628 violators. A further 18,549 were referred to their diplomatic missions to obtain travel documents, while 3,815 were referred to complete their travel reservations.The ministry said 31,398 expatriates, including 29,018 men and 2,380 women, are currently undergoing procedures to enforce legal measures for their violations.Security forces also arrested 22 people accused of helping violators by providing transportation, shelter or employment.The Ministry of Interior warned that anyone who facilitates the illegal entry of individuals into the Kingdom, transports them within Saudi Arabia, provides them with shelter or offers other assistance or services could face up to 15 years in prison and a fine of up to SR1 million.Vehicles used to transport violators and houses used to shelter them may also be confiscated, the ministry said.You use AI every day.
